deck: 40 Effective Java::02 Creating and Destroying Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 1 — what can a static factory do that a constructor cannot?
cards.back: Return an instance of any subtype, and reuse a cached instance
cards.extra: Boolean.valueOf returns the shared TRUE/FALSE constants. A constructor always returns a brand-new object of exactly that class.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
interface Shape { }
record Circle() implements Shape { } record Square() implements Shape { }
final class Shapes {
    static final Shape ONLY = new Circle();
    static Shape of(boolean cached) { return cached ? ONLY : new Square(); }   // subtype or cached
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 1 — what is the main drawback of static factories?
cards.back: A class with only a private constructor cannot be subclassed, and the methods are hard to find in Javadoc
cards.extra: Callers may not realise the factory exists. The book's fix is naming conventions: of, from, valueOf, getInstance.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
class Ex {
  private Ex() {}
  static Ex create() { return new Ex(); }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 2 — when should you reach for a builder instead of constructors or setters?
cards.back: When the class has many optional parameters
cards.extra: Telescoping constructors become unreadable past a few options; the setter (JavaBeans) pattern leaves the object mutable during construction.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
final class Config {
    int a, b, c, d;
    Config a(int v) { a = v; return this; }
    Config d(int v) { d = v; return this; }
}
Config cfg = new Config().a(1).d(4);   // many optional values: builder pattern

cards.front: Effective Java Item 2 — what does the JavaBeans setter pattern cost you?
cards.back: The object is mutable and inconsistent while being built, so it cannot be immutable or thread-safe
cards.extra: A builder keeps the built object immutable and validates once in build().
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
final class Bean {
    int a, b;
    void setA(int v) { a = v; }
    void setB(int v) { b = v; }
}
Bean x = new Bean(); x.setA(1);   // half-built, mutable state (1, 0)

cards.front: Effective Java Item 3 — which singleton implementation does Effective Java recommend?
cards.back: A single-element enum — immune to reflection and serialization attacks
cards.extra: The public-field and static-factory versions need extra code to survive serialization and reflection; the enum gets both for free.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
enum Singleton {
    INSTANCE;
    void work() { System.out.println("one instance"); }
    static void demo() { Singleton.INSTANCE.work(); }
}
// No public constructor: reflection and serialization cannot create a second one.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 3 — what testability problem do singletons create?
cards.back: You cannot substitute a mock unless the singleton implements an interface
cards.extra: Hard-wired global state makes tests order-dependent. The book accepts singletons only for genuinely unique components.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects
cards.example:
interface Clock { long now(); }
enum RealClock implements Clock { INSTANCE; public long now() { return System.currentTimeMillis(); } }
final class Client {
    static long read(Clock c) { return c.now(); }   // injectable: a mock can replace the singleton
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 4 — how do you make a utility class non-instantiable?
cards.extra: The private constructor also prevents subclassing, which is exactly what you want for a class that is only a bag of static methods.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword
cards.example:
final class Util {
    private Util() { throw new AssertionError(); }
    static int twice(int x) { return x + x; }
    static void demo() { System.out.println(twice(3)); }   // 6, no instance
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 5 — why is hard-wiring a resource in a static field or singleton a design error?
cards.back: The class becomes inflexible and untestable: the resource cannot be swapped
cards.extra: A spell checker bound to one dictionary cannot be tested with a stub. Dependency injection passes the resource in.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::05 Dependency Injection
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static final java.io.PrintStream LOG = System.out;
  void run() { LOG.println("hi"); }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 5 — what form of dependency injection does the item recommend?
cards.extra: Constructor injection makes the dependency visible in the signature and lets the field be final. A DI framework only automates the wiring.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::05 Dependency Injection
cards.example:
class Ex {
  private final java.io.PrintStream out;
  Ex(java.io.PrintStream out) { this.out = out; }
  void run() { out.println("injected"); }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 6 — why is new String("bikini") a mistake?
cards.back: It creates a new instance every time, while the literal reuses one pooled object
cards.extra: In a loop it allocates millions of identical objects. The literal is shorter, faster and does the same job.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
String a = "bikini";
String b = "bikini";
String c = new String("bikini");
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (a == c));   // true false

cards.front: Effective Java Item 6 — when is avoiding object creation the wrong optimisation?
cards.back: When it means hand-rolling a cache or pool for cheap objects
cards.extra: Caching costs memory and can leak. Modern JVMs allocate cheaply; the win is avoiding genuinely expensive work.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
Object cheap = new Object();
java.util.Map<Object, Object> pool = new java.util.HashMap<>();
pool.put("key", cheap);   // pooling a cheap object adds bookkeeping for no gain
System.out.println(pool.get("key") == cheap);

cards.front: Effective Java Item 7 — what causes the memory leak in the array-backed Stack?
cards.back: pop() shrinks the size but leaves the stale reference in the array
cards.extra: The element stays reachable while the array lives. Fix: elements[--size] = null; after reading the value.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
Object[] elements = new Object[16];
elements[0] = new Object();
int size = 1;
size--;   // pop(): elements[0] still holds the reference -> leak
elements[0] = null;   // what pop() must do

cards.front: Effective Java Item 7 — when do you actually need to null out references?
cards.back: When the class manages its own memory — arrays used as caches, registries, listener lists
cards.extra: A variable going out of scope drops its own reference. Nulling everywhere else is noise.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
Object[] cache = new Object[4];
cache[0] = new Object();
cache[0] = null;   // array cache: clear the removed slot
Object listener = new Object(); java.util.List<Object> ls = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
ls.add(listener); ls.remove(listener);   // listener registry: release it

cards.front: Effective Java Item 8 — why should you avoid finalizers and cleaners?
cards.back: They are unpredictable and slow: no guarantee they ever run; a finalizer can resurrect an object, a cleaner cannot resurrect the cleaned object
cards.extra: They are not C++ destructors. Java's GC already reclaims memory; a finalizer may run minutes later or never.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Resurrecting {
    static Object saved;
    @Override protected void finalize() throws Throwable { saved = this; }   // can resurrect
}
// No guarantee the finalizer or cleaner ever runs, or runs promptly.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 8 — what should replace finalizers for releasing resources?
cards.back: An explicit close() method (AutoCloseable), used with try-with-resources
cards.extra: Explicit close puts cleanup at a known point in the program instead of in the collector's hands.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Resource implements AutoCloseable {
    public void close() { System.out.println("cleaned up"); }
    static void demo() {
        try (Resource r = new Resource()) { System.out.println("use"); }   // close() at block exit
    }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 9 — why is try-with-resources better than try-finally?
cards.back: It closes every resource automatically and keeps the primary exception
cards.extra: Two resources mean nested try-finally blocks that lose the second exception; try-with-resources attaches it as suppressed.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (java.io.PrintWriter out = new java.io.PrintWriter("out.txt");
     java.io.Reader in = new java.io.FileReader("in.txt")) {
  out.println(in.read());
}
} }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 9 — what must a resource implement to be used in try-with-resources?
cards.extra: Any type whose close() can throw works, which is why streams and JDBC connections support it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
AutoCloseable res = new AutoCloseable() { public void close() { System.out.println("closed"); } };
try (AutoCloseable r = res) { System.out.println("using"); } catch (Exception e) { }   // AutoCloseable required
// Closeable is its subinterface and works too.
